style.summary:
style of A: Direct and decisive, with we and firm framing around deadlines and decisions, though the phrasing stutters as A searches for words.
style of B: Brief and agreeable, mostly backchannels like Yeah, with a turn that trails off mid-sentence.

A: A sets a direct, businesslike register that B follows rather than challenges.
A's directive framing of time pressure and required decisions gives A the tone of someone in charge.
A's question to B places B in the position of answering rather than steering.
B: B's relaxed, minimal replies set a low-pressure tone that A has to adapt to.
B's remark that the system will learn normalization is the framing A has to respond to.
B's willingness to say little leaves A carrying the burden of making the conversation productive.

A: A's blunt register is undercut by the stutters and restarts, which show A searching for footing while B holds steady.
The time pressure A invokes binds both speakers, and B's brief replies quietly leave A needing B's agreement to make the decisions.
A's question only works if B answers, and B's unfinished reply shows B decides how much to give.
B: A's businesslike framing, not B's agreeableness, decides how the exchange is run, so B's ease does not set the tone.
B's point about normalization is a passing remark that A steers away from in the next turn, so A controls where the technical thread goes.
B's silence cedes control, and A fills the space by setting the agenda.

content.summary:
content of A: Sets the agenda around time pressure, proposing conclusions, reductions in scope, and strong decisions about testing before next week.
content of B: Raises a technical point about features being normalized by the system itself, then mostly defers the decisions to A.

A: A's request to draw conclusions and cut scope is the concrete action the exchange turns on.
A ties the decisions to the deadline, which gives A's proposal its urgency.
A names testing choices as the outcome, so the substance of the talk is A's plan.
B: B's point that the features will be learned and normalized introduces the technical premise the discussion depends on.
B's technical framing shapes whether reductions are needed at all.
B's acknowledgments accept A's plan, so the content rests on B's agreement.

A: A's cut-and-decide plan needs B's technical sign-off to take effect, so B holds the veto.
The deadline binds both speakers, and B's technical premise is what decides which reductions are safe.
A names the outcome, but B's agreement is what makes it the group's plan, so B controls the substance.
B: B's premise is a remark A can set aside as the plan moves forward, so A's agenda stays the substance.
Whether reductions are needed is a judgment A makes once the plan is set, so B's framing does not decide it.
B's agreement is passive, and A's plan is the content the talk produces.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: Holds the floor for most substantive turns and drives the shift from discussion to decisions.
coordination of B: Gives short turns and is cut off, with a final turn that stops after Yeah I'd.

A: A holds the floor for the longest substantive turns.
A makes the transition from technical discussion to decisions with So do you.
A keeps B in short responses by asking pointed questions.
B: B's interjection about the system learning normalization redirects the turn in a way A must follow.
B's Yeah and Mmm backchannels let A keep going while B controls the tempo.
B's unfinished turn leaves the next move open, so B decides when the exchange passes on.

A: A's long turns are only possible while B yields, so B controls how much room A gets.
A's transition questions only move the exchange if B answers them, so B decides when the topic changes.
A's pointed questions can be left unanswered, and B's unfinished turn shows B can withhold the answer.
B: B's interjection is a single remark that A absorbs and moves past, so A still sets the flow.
B's backchannels are passive signals, and A decides when to keep the floor.
B's unfinished turn is simply left open, and A chooses whether to take the next turn.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: Asks B a direct question about their position, pulling B into the decision.
engagement of B: Shows attention through repeated Yeah and Mmm, but offers little new content of their own.

A: A's direct question to B draws B into the decision and makes B's position the one that matters.
A's concern about time pressure shows A is invested in the outcome.
A's push for decisions before next week shows strong investment in directing the work.
B: B's repeated acknowledgments show steady attention that keeps A engaged.
B's technical point about learned normalization shows real investment in the method.
B's willingness to let A carry the decisions reflects a focused stake in the outcome.

A: A's question is a prompt, but B's answer decides whether the decision is made, so B's engagement is the one that counts.
A's concern about time is shared by B, so it does not show A has more investment in the outcome.
A's push for decisions depends on B's agreement, so B's investment shapes what is decided.
B: B's acknowledgments are passive, so A's active questions show the stronger engagement.
B's technical point is a single remark, while A's plan shows sustained investment in the method.
B's willingness to defer is passive, so A's stake in the decisions is the one that drives the outcome.
